ev.waf_fc_namesake.elder.ok: An elder whispered the name into your ear, then spoke it aloud, and the griot repeated it for the whole village. The old people wept: "{g:He|She} has come back."
ev.waf_fc_namesake.marabout.ok: The marabout came to the naming himself and whispered a prayer into your ear. "One more pupil in our house," he said, and gave you a leather amulet with a written verse sewn inside.
ev.waf_fc_namesake.rich: A namesake from the rich house next door
ev.waf_fc_namesake.rich.ok: The rich neighbour accepted the honour gladly: he sent a ram for the feast and a length of indigo cloth. "The namesake of our house will want for nothing," he declared before everyone.
ev.waf_fc_namesake.title: Whose name will you bear
ev.waf_fc_namesake.text: On the seventh day you will be named – and given a namesake: the person you are named after, who will be like a second parent to you. The elders want you to have your {g:grandfather's|grandmother's} name – they say {g:his|her} spirit has come back to the house. Your father is thinking of the household of the marabout he studied with – naming you {g:after the teacher himself|after the teacher's mother}. Or a namesake could be chosen from a rich neighbour's house – someone generous and powerful.
ev.waf_fc_namesake.note: In West Africa a child is named on the seventh or eighth day. Children are often named after a grandparent – whose spirit, it is believed, has returned – or after a respected person, who becomes the child's namesake (among the Manden, togoma) and looks after "their" child for life with gifts and advice.
ev.waf_fc_namesake_elder.title: An old name
ev.waf_fc_namesake_elder.text: More and more often the elders call you to sit with them under the council tree. "You bear your {g:grandfather's|grandmother's} name," they say, "and {g:he|she} was wiser than all of us." Your age-mates are envious, and you are learning to keep silent and listen, as befits one in whom an ancestor has returned.
ev.waf_fc_namesake_marabout.title: The marabout's board
ev.waf_fc_namesake_marabout.text: The marabout whose household gave you your name kept his word: he took you into his school and asks no fee. From dawn you sit in the sand by his house, tracing Arabic letters on a wooden board and learning suras by heart, and in the evening you wash the board clean and wait for new lines.
ev.waf_fc_namesake_rich.title: A rich namesake
ev.waf_fc_namesake_rich.text: The wealthy house that gave you your name has not forgotten its namesake. When the time came for you to set yourself up, they sent a cow, a sack of millet and a string of cowries – "from your name".
ev.waf_fc_griot.gold.ok: Your father gave the griot gold dust wrapped in a rag and his best length of cloth. The griot sang till dawn, and in his song your name rang out as though you had already done something great.
ev.waf_fc_griot.kola: Kola nuts and a few cowries
ev.waf_fc_griot.kola.ok: The griot was given kola nuts and a string of cowries – what decent folk give. He sang what was owed and went on to the neighbours, not offended, but not lingering either.
ev.waf_fc_griot.refuse.ok: Your father said praise is for those with nothing to be proud of. The griot smiled, broke off his song halfway and left without a farewell.
ev.waf_fc_griot.title: The griot's song
ev.waf_fc_griot.text: Your family's griot came to the naming. He struck up on the balafon and sang of your ancestors – who fought whom, who fed whom in the hungry year – and now he waits for his gift. For a generous house a griot sings praises at every feast; a miser he will mock until the whole district is laughing.
ev.waf_fc_griot.note: Griots (jeli) were keepers of genealogies, singers and counsellors. In 1352 Ibn Battuta saw the griot Dugha at the court of the mansa of Mali, playing an instrument of wood and gourds. A praise song was rewarded generously, and a miser could be mocked so well that the jibe outlived him.
ev.waf_fc_griot_praise.title: Praise at the festival
ev.waf_fc_griot_praise.text: At a great festival the son of the old griot who sang at your naming spotted you in the crowd and began to sing of you – of your house's generosity, of your ancestors, and of you. People turned and nodded, and the old men said: that house knows how to show gratitude.
ev.waf_fc_griot_mock.title: A mocking song
ev.waf_fc_griot_mock.text: At someone else's wedding the griot who was once sent away empty-handed from your naming spotted you and struck up a ditty about a house where "praise is worth less than a kola nut". Everyone knew who was meant and roared with laughter, and for a long time your age-mates would hum the refrain at you.
